activity.lewis.title: Lewis Structure Builder
activity.lewis.desc: Drag electrons into the valence shell and build molecules.
activity.hybrid.title: Hybridization Lab
activity.hybrid.desc: Count electron groups and mix orbitals: sp, sp², sp³.
activity.crystal.title: Crystal Lattice Builder
activity.crystal.desc: Build unit cells, grow a lattice and make a material.
activity.organic.title: Organic Chemistry
activity.organic.desc: Functional groups, chirality, isomers and more.
activity.pharmacy.title: Pharmacy Applications
activity.pharmacy.desc: Salts, absorption, docking, stability and more.
privacy.notice: Your camera video stays on this device. Nothing is recorded or uploaded.
drnam.tip.1: Make a finger gun: aim with your index finger, then drop your thumb to shoot!
drnam.tip.2: Did you know? Atoms bond to reach a stable outer shell — usually 8 electrons.
drnam.tip.3: Try this: start with Easy, then challenge a friend in 2-player mode.
drnam.tip.4: Pharmacy link: the shape of a drug molecule decides how it fits its target.
drnam.tip.5: No camera? No problem — click with your mouse or tap the screen.
tutorial.aim.title: Aim
tutorial.aim.body: Point your index finger at the screen. The lime crosshair follows your fingertip. Aim at the target until it glows.
tutorial.shoot.title: Shoot to select
tutorial.shoot.body: Make a finger gun: index finger out, thumb up. Drop your thumb onto your finger to shoot. Hit all 3 targets!
tutorial.grab.title: Grab and drop
tutorial.grab.body: Pinch your thumb and index finger to grab the electron. Move it into the ring, then open your hand to drop it.
tutorial.mouse: Using a mouse? Click the targets and drag the electron.

lewis.level.easy: Fill the valence electrons, then join atoms with single bonds.
lewis.level.medium: Build covalent molecules with lone pairs and double or triple bonds.
lewis.level.hard: Ionic bonding: transfer electrons from the metal to the non-metal.
lewis.task.atom: How many valence electrons does {name} ({sym}) have? Drag that many electrons into the slots.
lewis.task.molecule: Build the Lewis structure of {name} ({formula}). Pairs between atoms are shared bonds; the rest are lone pairs.
lewis.task.ionic: Form {name} ({formula}): drag the valence electron(s) from the metal into the empty slots of the non-metal.
lewis.task.charge: Now give each ion its charge. What is the charge on {sym}?
lewis.count.q: First count: how many valence electrons are there in total in {formula}?
lewis.count.sum: Add the valence electrons of every atom: {sum}.
lewis.count.ok: Total = {n} valence electrons. Now drag them in!
lewis.hint.atom.many: Too many electrons: {sym} has only {n} valence electron(s), but you placed {got}.
lewis.hint.atom.few: Too few electrons: {sym} has {n} valence electron(s), but you placed {got}.
lewis.hint.many: Too many electrons around {sym}: it has {got}, but its shell holds only {target}.
lewis.hint.few: Octet not satisfied: {sym} has only {got} electrons around it and needs {target}. Shared pairs count for both atoms.
lewis.hint.unpaired: Electrons sit in pairs. Complete the half-filled pair (a bond or a lone pair).
lewis.hint.ion: {n} electron(s) still to transfer. The metal gives away all its valence electrons so the non-metal reaches 8.
lewis.hint.charge.metal: {sym} gave away {n} electron(s), so it has {n} more proton(s) than electrons: the charge is positive.
lewis.hint.charge.non: {sym} gained {n} electron(s), so it has {n} more electron(s) than protons: the charge is negative.
lewis.atom.why: {sym} has {n} valence electron(s). A full outer shell holds {target}.
lewis.reveal.title: The Lewis structure
lewis.reveal.shown: Answer shown — no points this time.
lewis.legend.bond: Line = shared pair (bond). Dots = lone pair.
lewis.legend.ion: Brackets and charge show each ion.
lewis.tip.atom: Did you know? For main-group atoms the group number tells you the valence electrons.
lewis.tip.molecule: Try this: count the total valence electrons, then share pairs until every atom has a full shell.
lewis.tip.multiple: Try this: if an atom is short of electrons, share two or three pairs — a double or triple bond.
lewis.tip.ionic: Did you know? Metals lose electrons and non-metals gain them. Opposite charges attract.
lewis.done.title: Level complete!
lewis.challenge.title: Mixed challenge
lewis.challenge.intro: Beat the clock! {n} mixed items in {s} seconds. Atoms, covalent molecules and ionic compounds are all mixed up.
lewis.duo: 2 Players: split-screen play arrives in Phase 5. For now, take turns.
lewis.error: Could not load the molecule data.
lewis.touchhint: No camera needed: drag electrons with your finger or mouse, or tap an electron and then tap a slot. Tap a placed electron to take it back.
lewis.colorhint: Each atom's electrons have their own colour. Watch how a shared pair is made from two different atoms.
lewis.hint.source: A shared pair is made of one electron from each atom. Put one {a} electron and one {b} electron in this bond.
pt.title: Periodic table
pt.tip: Tip: for main-group atoms, the group number tells you the valence electrons (group 1 = 1, group 17 = 7).
pt.poster.key.sym: Large letters: the element's symbol, with its name below.
pt.poster.key.mass: Bottom: atomic mass. Brackets mean the most stable isotope.
lewis.task.hidden: There are no guide marks: work out where every electron goes. The grey spare electrons are decoys.
lewis.task.ionic.free: Form {name} ({formula}): move the valence electron(s) from the metal onto the non-metal(s). There are no guide marks, and the grey spare electrons are decoys.
lewis.task.ionic.think: Now form {name}: move electrons from the metal(s) to the non-metal(s) so every atom has a full shell. No guide marks, and the grey spare electrons are decoys.
lewis.task.pick: Which atoms do you need to make {name}? Tap tiles to add atoms. Use the periodic table (top bar) to check valence electrons. Watch out for tiles that do not belong!
lewis.task.formula: What is the formula of {name}? The total positive and negative charges must cancel out.
lewis.task.charge.all: Now give each ion its charge.
lewis.pick.ok: Right atoms! Now move the electrons.
lewis.tip.pick: Try this: the metal gives away its valence electrons and each non-metal takes just enough to reach 8. Balance the electrons given and taken.
lewis.hint.spare: A grey spare electron belongs to no atom, so it cannot be used. Only electrons from the atoms can move or be shared.
lewis.hint.ion.many: Too many electrons on {sym}: it would have {got}, but a full shell holds only {target}.
lewis.hint.pick.missing: An element is missing: {name} is made from a metal and a non-metal.
lewis.hint.pick.count: {metal} gives {mv} electron(s) per atom and each {nonmetal} takes {need}. Choose the numbers of atoms so that electrons given = electrons taken.
lewis.hint.formula: The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. Add up the charges of your ions.
hybrid.error: Could not load the molecule data.
hybrid.task.count: Count the electron groups around the highlighted {sym} atom in {name}. Shoot every bond line and every lone pair of {sym}.
hybrid.hint.decoy: Those lone pairs belong to {sym}, not the highlighted atom. Count only the groups around the central atom.
hybrid.hint.double: The {a}–{b} bond has {count} lines selected. A double or triple bond counts as ONE electron group, however many lines it has.
hybrid.hint.missed.lp: You missed a lone pair on {sym}. Lone pairs are electron groups too.
hybrid.hint.missed.bond: You missed the bond between {sym} and {other}.
hybrid.hint.missed.h: You missed a hydrogen on {sym}. Each bonded atom is a group.
hybrid.task.mix: {sym} has {n} electron groups, so it needs {n} hybrid orbitals. Which orbitals will you mix? Drag them into the mixer (or tap them), then press Mix!
hybrid.hint.no-s: Every set of hybrid orbitals needs exactly one s orbital.
hybrid.hint.few-p: {groups} hybrid orbitals need 1 s + {need} p orbitals, but you used only {got} p.
hybrid.hint.many-p: Too many p orbitals: {groups} groups need 1 s + {need} p, and you used {got} p.
hybrid.hint.d: d orbitals do not take part here: only s and p orbitals mix for these atoms.
hybrid.task.pi: The {k} p orbital(s) that were not mixed are left over. They make π bonds by overlapping side by side. Label every bond line around {sym}: σ or π. Tap a chip to change it.
hybrid.task.pi.none: The {k} leftover p orbital(s) on {sym} are empty: there is no π bond here.
hybrid.hint.unlabelled: Label every bond line with σ or π first.
hybrid.hint.sigma: Every bond has exactly one σ bond. The {a}–{b} bond (order {order}) is 1 σ + {pi} π.
hybrid.task.label: {name}: shoot each numbered atom and label it sp, sp² or sp³. Count its electron groups first.
hybrid.check.label: Check all labels
hybrid.miss.multiple: A double bond counts once, not twice.
hybrid.task.done: {name}: {sym} has {n} electron groups, so it is {h} and the shape is {shape} ({angle}). Rotate the molecule!
hybrid.task.drug.done: {name}: every numbered atom, with its electron groups.
hybrid.info.title: What to remember
hybrid.view.hint: Drag to rotate (or grab with your hand).
hybrid.view.nowebgl: 3D is not available on this device. The 2D structure and the table show the same result.
hybrid.table.title: Summary
hybrid.why.title: Why hybridization?
hybrid.why.1: Forming more bonds makes the atom more stable, so s and p orbitals mix to make equal hybrid orbitals that bond well.
hybrid.why.2: Electron groups spread as far apart as they can to reduce repulsion. That decides the shape and the angle.
hybrid.why.3: π bonds need unmixed p orbitals, so each π bond leaves one p orbital out of the mix.
hybrid.limits: Model limit: heavier atoms such as S in H₂S (bond angle about 92°) show little hybridization. The model works best for C, N, O and B.
hybrid.tip.count: Did you know? A double or triple bond points in one direction, so it counts as one electron group.
hybrid.tip.mix: Try this: the number of hybrid orbitals always equals the number of electron groups.
hybrid.tip.pi: Did you know? A σ bond is end-to-end overlap. A π bond is side-by-side overlap of p orbitals.
hybrid.tip.pi.none: Leftover p orbitals can be empty, as in BF₃: that is why BF₃ is electron-hungry.
hybrid.tip.label: Pharmacy link: the shape of a drug molecule decides how it fits its target, and hybridization sets that shape.
hybrid.mixed.left: {p} p orbital(s) are left over and glow.
hybrid.mixed.none: No p orbitals are left over, so there is no π bond.
crystal.error: Could not load the lattice data.
crystal.error3d: This activity needs 3D graphics (WebGL), which this browser cannot provide. Please try another browser or device.
crystal.view.hint: Drag the cube to rotate it (or grab it with your hand).
crystal.task.build: Build the {name} ({abbr}) unit cell. Tap the rings to place particles where they belong, or drag the particle from the tray onto a ring. Rotate the cube to see every side.
crystal.task.nacl: Build one NaCl unit cell from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Pick an ion in the tray, then tap the rings (or drag the ion onto a ring). Ions of opposite charge alternate: no two Na⁺ or two Cl⁻ side by side. Rotate the cube to check every layer.
crystal.tip.build: Did you know? A particle at a corner is shared by 8 touching cells, so only ⅛ of it belongs to each cell.
crystal.tip.nacl: Pharmacy link: a saline drip is salt water. When the NaCl crystal dissolves, the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions separate and carry electric charge.
crystal.hint.missing: You are missing {n} particle(s) on {kind} sites.
crystal.hint.extra: {n} particle(s) sit on {kind} sites, but a {name} cell has none there.
crystal.hint.wrong-ion: {n} ion(s) are the wrong kind. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ must alternate: every ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.
crystal.task.ask: Your {name} cell is built! Now count what belongs to it.
crystal.tip.ask: Try this: count shared particles as fractions. Corner = ⅛, edge = ¼, face = ½, centre = 1.
crystal.q.ppc: How many particles belong to ONE {abbr} unit cell? (Shared particles count as fractions.)
crystal.q.cn: What is the coordination number: how many nearest neighbours touch each particle?
crystal.hint.ppc: Corner particles are shared by 8 cells (⅛ each), face particles by 2 cells (½ each), and a particle in the centre belongs wholly to the cell (1). Add them up.
crystal.hint.cn: Count the particles that touch ONE particle. Tap Show neighbours to see them.
crystal.task.identify: Look at this unit cell and rotate it. Which lattice is it?
crystal.q.identify: Which lattice is this unit cell?
crystal.tip.identify: Try this: look for a particle in the centre of the cube, and for particles in the middle of each face.
crystal.hint.identify: Check two things: is there a particle in the centre of the cube? Is there one in the middle of each face?
crystal.task.match: Make a material! Choose a structure tab, then tap the property that matches it. Each structure gets one property. One property is a decoy that matches none of them.
crystal.tip.match: Think about how the particles are held together, and whether any ions or electrons can move.
crystal.props.title: Properties for {name}:
crystal.hint.match.missing: Give every structure a property first.
crystal.hint.match.wrong: Think about how the particles are held in {name} ({bonding}) and whether any electrons or ions are free to move.
crystal.task.quiz: Short quiz about NaCl and materials. Rotate the NaCl lattice for clues.
crystal.tip.quiz: Pharmacy link: many drugs are salts. How a crystal is built decides how it dissolves.
crystal.task.match.done: You made four materials! Tap a structure to see it again.
crystal.quiz.done.note: Well done: you can now explain why NaCl is brittle, why metals bend, and why graphite conducts.
crystal.info.title: What to remember
crystal.task.done: {name} ({abbr}): see the unit cell, then repeat it to fill space.
crystal.repeat.title: A lattice!
crystal.repeat.note: Repeating the unit cell in every direction fills space. This block has {n} particles.
crystal.tip.done: Did you know? A crystal lattice is just one unit cell repeated again and again in 3D.
crystal.touchhint: No camera needed: tap a ring to place or remove a particle, and drag the cube with your finger or mouse to rotate it.
